'''Yousef Alavi''' (March 19, 1928 – May 21, 2013)<ref name=":0">{{citation|url=http://obits.mlive.com/obituaries/kalamazoo/obituary.aspx?pid=164943570|title=Yousef Alavi|newspaper=[[Kalamazoo Gazette]]|date=May 23, 2013}}.</ref> was an Iranian-American mathematician, based at [[Western Michigan University]] (WMU), who specialized in [[graph theory]]. He received his [[PhD]] from [[Michigan State University]] in 1958,<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=15173}}</ref> and his career at WMU lasted until 1996. Alavi was a frequent collaborator with [[Don R. Lick]] and [[Jiuqiang Liu]] (both of [[Eastern Michigan University]]) as well as with [[Paul Erdős]],<!-- MathSciNet collaboration data --> and in 1987, the Michigan Section of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] (MAA) awarded him its first annual Distinguished Service Award. 

== Early life and education (1928–1958) ==
Alavi was born in the city of [[Ahvaz]] in [[Pahlavi Iran]] in 1928.<ref name=":0" /> He moved to the [[United States]] in 1948.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Yousef Alavi obituary {{!}} News {{!}} Western Michigan University |url=https://wmich.edu/news/2013/06/7363 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20260114220255/https://wmich.edu/news/2013/06/7363 |archive-date=January 14, 2026 |access-date=January 14, 2026 |website=wmich.edu |language=en}}</ref> There, he earned a bachelor's degree in [[electrical engineering]] from [[Michigan State University]] in 1953, a master's in math from the same school in 1955, and a PhD in 1958.<ref name=":1" />

== Career (1958–1996) ==
He was a professor of mathematics at WMU from 1958 until his retirement in 1996;<ref>[http://www.wmich.edu/math/emeriti%20faculty.html Emeritus faculty] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090702075512/http://www.wmich.edu/math/emeriti%20faculty.html |date=2009-07-02 }}, Western Michigan University mathematics department.</ref> he chaired the department from 1989 to 1992.<ref>[http://www.wmich.edu/math/history.htm History of the department] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090301032938/http://www.wmich.edu/math/history.htm |date=2009-03-01  }}, Western Michigan University mathematics department.</ref>

Alavi was known for complaining that "this is highly irregular!" He was also a frequent host for Erdős on his visits to Western Michigan. On one of these visits, these two things came together: he made his usual complaint at a time when Erdős and [[Ronald Graham]] were present. This sparked a discussion on what it might mean for a graph to be highly irregular, kicking off a line of joint research on [[highly irregular graph]]s through which Alavi obtained [[Erdős number]] one.<ref>{{citation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_GsQiXvfNWkC&pg=PA197|page=197|title=My Brain is Open: The Mathematical Journeys of Paul Erdős|first=Bruce|last=Schechter|publisher=Simon and Schuster|year=2000|isbn=9780684859804}}</ref>

In 1987, he received the first Distinguished Service Award of the Michigan Section of the MAA due to his 30 years of service to the section; at that time, the Michigan House and Senate issued a special resolution honoring him.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MAA Michigan Section |url=http://sections.maa.org/michigan/history.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/iGlYK |archive-date=17 March 2026 |access-date=17 March 2026 |website=sections.maa.org}}</ref>

=== Research ===
In 1987, Alavi, Erdős, [[Paresh J. Malde]], and [[Allen J. Schwenk]] studied the [[vertex independence sequence]] <math>a_1, \dots, a_m</math> of an [[undirected graph]] where ''m'' is the maximal order of any [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]], where <math>a_i</math> denotes the number of independent sets on exactly ''i'' vertices.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Alavi |first=Yousef |last2=Malde |first2=Paresh J. |last3=Schwenk |first3=Allen J. |last4=Erdos |first4=Paul |date=1987 |title=The Vertex Independence Sequence of a Graph Is Not Constrained |url=https://renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1987-33.pdf |journal=Congressus Numerantium |volume=58 |pages=15-23}}</ref> By taking the [[Join (graph theory)|join]] of several [[complete graphs]], they were able to show that this sequence can realize any possible [[permutation]].<ref name=":4" />

That same year, Alavi, Erdős, [[A. J. Boals]], [[Gary Chartrand]], and [[Ortrud Oellermann]] also introduced the notion of an [[ascending subgraph decomposition]], where a graph is decomposed into a sequence of [[Subgraph (graph theory)|subgraphs]] such that each of those graphs is isomorphic to a subgraph of the next graph. They conjectured that every finite graph admits an ascending subgraph decomposition, and verified it for the cases of all [[Path (graph theory)|paths]], all [[Cycle (graph theory)|cycles]], and all graphs with at most 6 vertices.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Alavi |first=Yousef |last2=Boals |first2=A. J. |last3=Chartrand |first3=Gary |last4=Erdos |first4=Paul |last5=Oellermann |first5=Ortrud R. |date=1987 |title=The Ascending Subgraph Decomposition Problem |url=https://combinatorica.hu/~p_erdos/1987-31.pdf |journal=Congressus Numerantium |volume=58 |pages=7-14}}</ref>

In 1991, Alavi, Erdős, [[Mehdi Behzad]], and [[Don R. Lick]] introduced the notion of the [[double vertex graph]] of any graph.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Alavi |first=Yousef |last2=Lick |first2=Don R. |last3=Liu |first3=Jiuqiang |date=2002-12-01 |title=Survey of Double Vertex Graphs |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s003730200055 |journal=Graphs and Combinatorics |language=en |volume=18 |issue=4 |pages=709–715 |doi=10.1007/s003730200055 |issn=1435-5914|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Further research involving Alavi, Lick, and [[Jiuqiang Liu]] in 1993 and 1994 eventually led to a classification of which [[Hamiltonian graphs]] also have Hamiltonian double vertex graphs.<ref name=":5" /> In particular, the double vertex graph of the [[complete bipartite graph]] ''K(m, n)'' is not Hamiltonian unless the equation <math>(m - n)^2 = m + n</math> holds.<ref name=":5" />

== Death and legacy ==
Before his death, Alavi had been dedicated to his wife and son, both of whom ended up surviving him.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |date=October 2013 |title=Mathematics People |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201309/rnoti-p1181.pdf |url-status=live |journal=[[Notices of the AMS]] |pages=1184 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260114220308/https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201309/rnoti-p1181.pdf |archive-date=January 14, 2026}}</ref> He was remembered for possessing "great energy", "kindness", and "good humor".<ref name=":2" />

Alavi died on May 21, 2013;<ref>{{Cite web |title=Yousef Alavi Obituary (2013) - Kalamazoo, MI - Kalamazoo Gazette |url=https://obits.mlive.com/us/obituaries/kalamazoo/name/yousef-alavi-obituary?id=19587080 |access-date=January 14, 2026 |website=Legacy.com}}</ref> his health had been worsening for several months prior.<ref name=":2" /> A private funeral was held for him at the [[Riverside Cemetery (Michigan)|Riverside Cemetery]] at noon on May 23,<ref name=":0" /> and a memorial service was held for him on June 29 in the [[Kanley Chapel]].<ref name=":1" />

In remembrance of Alavi, the "Yousef Alavi Memorial Symposium" was held from October 24 to 25, 2013, on the sixth floor of the [[Everett Tower]] at WMU, as well as the [[Fetzer Center]]. It was free and open to the public.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Yousef Alavi to be remembered during math symposium {{!}} News {{!}} Western Michigan University |url=https://wmich.edu/news/2013/10/10358 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140831191821/https://wmich.edu/news/2013/10/10358 |archive-date=August 31, 2014 |access-date=January 14, 2026 |website=wmich.edu |language=en}}</ref> Speakers included [[Fan Chung]] and [[Ronald Graham]], both of the [[University of California, San Diego]].<ref name=":3" />
